name: Wendy Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at Brightwell Autos by half seven, a six-bay independent garage that Gloria has owned for twenty years. Most of my day is diagnostics, especially hybrids, because I'm the one who doesn't mind the electrical side. I plug in the scan tool, ask an AI assistant to pull up the wiring diagram and known faults, and then I go and find the broken thing myself, which is the fun part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What wears me out is the customer who's read three forums and wants me to replace the part they picked. What I love is when a car three other garages gave up on starts first time. I'm 27, I live with my boyfriend Kofi, no kids, and I've got about nine months of wages put away, so honestly I'm in a good spot right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds a lot like now, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at the pub quiz: the AI is a good apprentice that never gets tired, but it can't feel a wheel bearing grumble. I'd probably post a little told-you-so about all the hype. Gloria would be pleased, because she never bought into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the tools and I was hoping they'd get better. My job's safe in that picture, my pay's good, and there's a garage on every corner hiring. So it means more of the same, which isn't bad at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my hybrid and electric car courses, because the cars are changing whether AI does or not. I'd push Gloria to get a second high-voltage workstation this year so we stop turning away electric cars. And I'd keep putting a fifth of my pay into savings, because Kofi and I want a house deposit within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored by the idea, if I'm honest, but bored is fine when you've got a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a house deposit. How close are you, and does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're about halfway, and in this picture nothing changes, we just keep going. Kofi does sound work for events, so it's gig to gig, and my pay is the steady one in our house. That's the only pressure I really feel, being the reliable wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the garage you'd worry about, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Paul on the front desk, because the booking system already writes half his emails. Even in a boring world the dull bits of his job get eaten a little. But he's sixty-one and has big plans for his vegetable patch, so he'd laugh at me for worrying.

say: The AI is a **good apprentice**, but it can't feel a fault in a wheel bearing.
She'd happily post a little **told-you-so** about all the hype.
think: She'd be a little **disappointed**, because she enjoys the tools and hoped they'd improve.
Her job, pay and **local demand** stay solid, so more of the same suits her.
do: Keep taking **hybrid and electric** car courses, because the cars change regardless of AI.
Push Gloria (the owner) for a second **high-voltage workstation** this year.
Keep saving **a fifth of pay** toward a house deposit within three years.
feel: **Calm** and slightly bored, which she says is fine with a good job.
S0.quote: The AI is a good apprentice that never gets tired, but it can't feel a wheel bearing grumble.
fieldNote: She treats AI as an everyday **workshop tool** and sounds let down when it stalls.
Her one real pressure is being the **steady wage** while her boyfriend Kofi works gig to gig.
She worries about Paul on the **front desk** before herself, even in the mildest picture.

steps.text: Keep diagnosing hybrids at Brightwell Autos on the same hours
Finish the high-voltage electric car course this spring
Put a fifth of each pay packet into the house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, this one I can actually picture. Half of it is already happening at Brightwell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: learn the tools or get left behind, and I'd mean it kindly. At work I'd tell the younger mechanics that the scan tool plus the AI is now the job, not an extra. Online I'd probably share the courses I've done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The thinking parts of a garage, like quoting, ordering parts and answering customers, get done by software, and the person who's left in a garage is the one who can actually fix the car and read what the software says. I'm that person, so I'd expect more work and maybe a pay rise, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask Gloria to make me diagnostics lead, with a raise, since I'd be the one setting up the new systems. I'd do the ADAS calibration course, that's the cameras and radar in the windscreen and bumpers, because every windscreen job needs it now. And I'd leave my savings where they are rather than spending the raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually, a bit excited. There's a small guilty feeling about Paul, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a small guilty feeling about Paul. What happens to him in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this one I think Gloria doesn't replace him when he retires, and the booking software and parts ordering just absorb his job. I'd feel bad cheering about AI in front of him. I'd probably help him learn the new system so his last couple of years aren't miserable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting as a mechanic now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ama asked me exactly that last month. I told her to do it, but to go straight for electrics and diagnostics, not just oil changes. The mechanic who only swaps parts by the book is the one the software and the quick-fit chains squeeze first.

say: **Learn the tools** or get left behind, and she means that kindly.
The scan tool plus the AI is now **the job**, not an extra.
think: Software takes **quoting and ordering**, leaving the person who actually fixes the car.
That person is her, so she expects **more work** and maybe a raise.
do: Ask Gloria to make her **diagnostics lead** with a raise in the first year.
Take the **ADAS calibration** course for windscreen cameras and radar.
Leave her **savings untouched** instead of spending any raise.
feel: A little **guilty** about Paul, whose desk job gets absorbed.
S1.quote: The person who's left in a garage is the one who can actually fix the car and read what the software says.
fieldNote: She reads Steady Disruption as a **promotion**, because the thinking work moving to software suits her.
Her guilt about **Paul** is real but doesn't change her plans.
Her advice to young starters is specific: go for **electrics and diagnostics**.

steps.text: Set up the new AI booking and diagnostic systems at Brightwell Autos
Take the ADAS camera and radar calibration course this year
Bank any pay rise instead of spending it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say mechanics are fine for a bit, because the robots come later, and I'd mostly believe it. I'd tell people at work not to panic. Online I'd probably stay quiet, because everyone would be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job is gone in 2028. The AI would diagnose better than me, so I'm just the hands doing what it says, and hands are cheap. Then by 2031 even the hands have a robot version, and I'm 32 with a skill nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop thinking of myself as a car mechanic and start thinking of myself as someone who fixes machines. I'd look at the companies putting robots into garages and warehouses and try to get on their service teams early, because someone has to repair the robots for a while. I'd also hold off on the house, because a mortgage on a job with a three-year clock is a bad bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and I'm young, so it's not panic, but the floor moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the house. How would that conversation with Kofi go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be relieved, honestly, he's always been more nervous about the mortgage than me. The hard bit is we'd planned to try for kids in about four years, and I'd want to know what I'm doing for work first. So the house and the family both slide back a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots would need repairing for a while. How long do you think that lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, nobody does. Maybe until the robots can fix each other, which might be quick in this picture. That's the bit that keeps me up, that I'd be retraining for a job with its own clock on it.

say: Mechanics are **fine for a bit**, because the robots come about three years later.
She'd tell coworkers **not to panic** and stay quiet online.
think: The **thinking side** of her job goes in 2028, leaving her as cheap hands.
By 2031 robots do the **hands-on work** too, when she's 32.
do: Apply to **robot service teams** for garages and warehouses before 2028.
Hold off on **buying a house**, since a mortgage on a three-year clock is risky.
Push back plans for **children** until her next job is clear.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, because she's young and has savings.
S2.quote: By 2031 even the hands have a robot version, and I'm 32 with a skill nobody needs.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** between AI and robots as her window to move.
Her public calm hides a private view that her **diagnostic skill** loses value in 2028.
Even her fallback, **repairing robots**, feels to her like it has its own clock.

steps.text: Apply to robot service teams at warehouse and garage firms before 2028
Put the house purchase and plans for children back a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to actually do something, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where people who plan ahead come out okay. At work I'd tell Gloria we should get ahead of it rather than wait. I'd post the courses again, probably annoyingly often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three for the robots means I've got about eight years as a hands-on mechanic, until I'm 35. The thinking parts, like the diagnosis I'm proud of, change by 2031, but I can ride that by being the best at working with the AI. It's enough runway to retrain properly instead of grabbing whatever's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up this year for a part-time electrical engineering diploma, two evenings a week, which takes about three years. I'd keep working full time at Brightwell and save the overtime money. And we'd still buy the house, just a smaller one, with a smaller mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way that gets me moving. It feels like a deadline, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two evenings a week on top of full-time garage work. Is that realistic for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tiring, but I did my vocational certificate while working at a tyre place, so I know I can. Kofi cooks on those nights, that's the deal we'd make. The real cost is weekends, I'd lose most of them for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change course in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the robots arriving early, say in 2032, I'd skip straight to working for whoever installs them. I'd watch the trade magazines and the big chain garages, because they'd get the robots first. Small garages like Brightwell would be last, which buys a bit more time.

say: People who **plan ahead** come out okay in this one.
She'd tell Gloria the garage should **get ahead** of it rather than wait.
think: She reckons on **about eight years** of hands-on work, until she's 35.
Five years is enough runway to **retrain properly** instead of grabbing anything.
do: Start a part-time **electrical engineering diploma**, two evenings a week, this year.
Keep working **full time** at Brightwell and save the overtime money.
Buy a **smaller house** with a smaller mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it feels like a deadline rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years plus three for the robots means I've got about eight years as a hands-on mechanic, until I'm 35.
fieldNote: She does the **arithmetic** out loud: AI by 2031, robots by 2034, so eight years.
She has **studied while working** before, which makes her plan believable.
She expects **big chain garages** to get robots first and small ones last.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time electrical engineering diploma, two evenings a week
Save all overtime pay from Brightwell Autos
Buy a smaller house with a smaller mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's most of my thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. At work and online I'd say the same thing, that a decade is plenty of time if you start now and don't wait for the boss or the government. Gloria would roll her eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is actually the one I'd find hardest to stay sharp for. With two years you move because you're scared. With ten, it's easy to keep saying next year. Then suddenly I'm 39 and the robots are a year off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself checkpoints: diploma done by 30, working on robots or electrical systems by 33. I'd buy the house as planned in three years and we'd try for kids around then too. I'd keep a running list on my phone of every task at Brightwell that the AI already does, so I can see the change coming instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a nagging feeling that I'll get lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably myself, honestly, if I had ten years and wasted them. I'd also be cross with the carmakers, who already lock us out of their software, because they'd make the robots just as closed. The government I don't expect much from either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kofi say about the checkpoints?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh, because I do this with everything, I had a spreadsheet for our last holiday. But he'd hold me to it. He's the one who'd ask on my thirtieth birthday whether the diploma's done.

say: A decade means **nobody has an excuse**, so start now.
Don't wait for **the boss or government** to say what to do.
think: Ten years is the hardest stretch to **stay sharp** for.
She fears saying **next year** until she's 39 and robots are a year off.
do: Set **checkpoints**: diploma by 30, working on robots or electrical systems by 33.
Buy the house and **try for kids** in about three years, as planned.
Keep a **phone list** of every Brightwell task the AI already does.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with a nagging fear that she'll get **lazy** about it.
S4.quote: With two years you move because you're scared. With ten, it's easy to keep saying next year.
fieldNote: Her biggest risk in the slow version is her own **complacency**, not the technology.
She blames **carmakers** for locking software and expects robots to be just as closed.
She uses **checkpoints and lists** to manage change, and her boyfriend Kofi holds her to them.

steps.text: Finish the electrical engineering diploma by age 30
Move into robot or electrical systems work by age 33
Buy the house and try for children in about three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to retrain before the hands-on side goes too. What would help is cheap, fast courses run with the robot makers, so a mechanic can learn to service the new machines while still earning. And making carmakers share their repair software, so small garages like Brightwell aren't locked out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in the trade. I've spent ten years proving I can do this job to customers who ask for one of the men. If garage robots arrive just as I've finally stopped having to prove myself, that would be a very particular kind of annoying.

headlineQuote: If garage robots arrive just as I've finally stopped having to prove myself, that would be a very particular kind of annoying.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old **hybrid diagnostics** mechanic at Brightwell Autos, a six-bay independent garage.
She uses **AI tools daily** and sees Steady Disruption as a chance for promotion.
Her **steady wage** matters at home because her boyfriend Kofi works gig to gig.
In the fast AGI picture she would **delay the house** and children and chase robot service work.
With more warning she plans a **part-time diploma** and fears only her own complacency.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to retrain before robots reach hands-on work.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast **courses with robot makers** so mechanics can retrain while still earning.
Making carmakers **share repair software** so small garages aren't locked out.
